# Economic Focus **Current account adds to export woes** In September, Japan’s current account slipped into deficit for the first time in more than three decades, recording a shortfall of 142 billion yen. The shift in trade balance from surplus to deficit, following last year’s natural disasters, is well reported but recent developments in the current account raise yet more concerns about the structural drivers of Japan’s GDP growth going forward. With a shrinking working age population and a current account deficit, there are real concerns about Japan’s ability to pay back its sovereign debt – estimated at 250 per cent of GDP (compared to Greece’s 180 per cent). Furthermore, data also suggests that underlying geo-political tensions with China are having an impact on Japan’s exports to China. ## **Japanese current account (Billions of yen) Yen (TWI) and Japanese exports (Billions of yen)** 3000 8000 100

**Is Japan’s sovereign debt position sustainable?** The switch in Japan’s net trade position from surplus to deficit last year did not bring about a significant depreciation in the yen. In fact the yen is now 5 per cent higher on a trade weighted basis than in March 2011. The current account was a contributing factor, which until September had been in surplus as ‘net factor income’ and ‘cash transfers’ (expatriated profits) were offsetting the trade deficit. Japan is one of the most indebted nations in the world with public debt estimated around 250 per cent of GDP. With a shrinking and aging population, the sustainability of this debt must be questioned if the current account deficit persists. Is Japan set to be the world’s next major sovereign debt crisis? Economic Focus **Trade deficit: not just an export story** The current strength of the yen is eroding the competitiveness of Japanese exports. Coupled with weak demand from key export destinations – such as Europe and the US – exports have remained fairly flat over the past two and a half years. On the import side of the equation, the import bill is also being driven by two factors: (i) increased commodity imports to support the reconstruction effort after last year’s tsunami; and (ii) the doubling of the LNG import bill due to the shutdown of nuclear power generation.The implications of the current account and trade deficits are clear – GDP contracted 0.9% in Q3 (quarter-on-quarter). Is this deterioration temporary? Well, some nuclear capacity has come back online and continuation of this t

rend will of course further reduce Japan’s fuel import requirement (Japan’s stance on nuclear should become clearer after the snap parliamentary election in December). And the bulk of tsunami reconstruction will be completed soon, reducing the need to import construction materials. However, the export outlook is less clear cut. ## **Origin of China’s machinery and electronic imports (% of total)** 50%

Japan’s trade with China has deteriorated significantly of late. Assessing the changing origin of China’s imports reveals an interesting story – Japan appears to be losing market share to Taiwan and more recently Korea. This suggests that a geo-political dispute between Japan and China has led to China reducing imports from Japan – worsening Japan’s already painful export decline. China has seemingly been able to easily switch between suppliers, as Japan, Taiwan and Korea continue to account for a steady 42% of its imports of machinery and electronics. **China turning the corner** In contrast we see a more positive outlook for China. Positive economic data has emerged from China recently, supporting our expectation that GDP growth has started to accelerate. Government revenue grew 14 per cent annually in October, an indication that economic activity is picking up. Lead indicators in manufacturing have also made a significant breakthrough, with the PMI moving into expansionary territory for the first time since September 2011. On the basis of recent indicators we expect that China’s new leadership will see growth accelerate to 8.4% next year.
